title: Mā chido mṛtyo: a prayer to Death to spare strength, children and life
theme: Death, addressed as the fierce one who watches all people, is asked not to cut the worshipper off, not to strike, not to take away his strength, his children or his life; the worshippers offer him oblations.

words.context: With an aorist injunctive it forbids: P. 3.3.175 (माङि लुङ्)
The anonymous commentator: «मा विच्छेदय» — do not sever
The anonymous commentator: «मा वधीर्मा हिंसय» — do not harm
The anonymous commentator: «शारीरं बलं» — bodily strength
The anonymous commentator: «मा पीडय» — do not afflict
The anonymous commentator: «मा चोरव» — do not steal

words.gram: verb, reduplicated aorist injunctive 2nd sg. active
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «मा रीरिषो मा हिंसय» — do not harm
The anonymous commentator: «हे उग्र क्रूर» — O cruel one
The anonymous commentator: «नृन्प्राणिनश्चष्टे पुण्यपापरीक्षायै पश्यतीति नृचक्षास्तं नृचक्षसम्» — who looks at living beings to examine their merit and sin

words.meaning: may we worship, we would serve
words.role: main verb of the closing clause
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «विधेम परिचरेम» — let us serve

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes o: chidaḥ mṛtyo → chido mṛtyo.

sandhi.type: visarga after ī before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: A visarga after a vowel other than a or ā becomes r before a voiced sound: vadhīḥ mā → vadhīr mā.

sandhi.type: final m before a consonant; visarga after a
sandhi.rule: balam becomes balaṃ before v; vivṛhaḥ becomes vivṛho before m.

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a vowel; visarga after u before a vowel
sandhi.rule: rīriṣaḥ before ā loses its visarga and stands in hiatus (rīriṣa āyuḥ); āyuḥ before u becomes āyur (āyur ugra).

morphology.note: An aorist without the augment (an injunctive), as always after the prohibitive mā: P. 6.4.74 (न माङ्योगे). The same holds for vadhīḥ, vivṛhaḥ, pramoṣīḥ and rīriṣaḥ: five prohibitions, all aorist injunctives.
Reduplicated aorist of √riṣ, ‘harm’: the reduplication rī- with long vowel is the Vedic causative-type aorist.
The enclitic accusative of the second person, as in the Veda generally.

translation.literal: Do not cut [me] off, O Death; do not strike; do not tear away my strength; do not carry [it] off. Do not harm my offspring, [my] life, O fierce one. We would worship you, the watcher of people, with oblation.
translation.readable: Death, do not cut me off, do not strike me down, do not tear away my strength or carry it off. Fierce one, do not harm my children or my life. With offerings we would serve you, who watch over all people.

anvaya: हे मृत्यो मा छिदः मा वधीः मे बलम् मा विवृहः मा प्रमोषीः । हे उग्र मे प्रजाम् आयुः [च] मा रीरिषः । नृचक्षसम् त्वा हविषा विधेम ।
syntax: Five prohibitions, each mā with an aorist injunctive (chidaḥ, vadhīḥ, vivṛhaḥ, pramoṣīḥ, rīriṣaḥ), addressed to Death in the vocative (mṛtyo, ugra). The objects are given only for the third and fifth (balam; prajām and āyuḥ). The verse closes with a first person plural optative (vidhema) whose object is tvā, qualified by nṛcakṣasam, with the instrumental haviṣā.

ambiguities.topic: what is not to be cut off or struck
ambiguities.note: The text gives no object for chidaḥ and vadhīḥ. The anonymous commentator supplies them: for vadhīḥ «अस्मत्सत्कर्मानुष्ठानं» (our performance of good works), and for pramoṣīḥ «अस्मदीयपरलोकसाधनं» (our means to the next world). Read without him, the objects may simply be the speaker himself.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: As printed the first half has 19 syllables (mā chido mṛtyo mā vadhīr mā me balaṃ vivṛho mā pramoṣīḥ) and the second 22 (11 + 11). The first half falls three syllables short of the triṣṭubh norm of 22; the edition records the count and does not emend.

beginner: This short prayer speaks directly to Death. It asks five things in a row, each with the word for "do not": do not cut me off, do not strike, do not tear away my strength, do not carry it off, do not harm my children or my life. Death is called "fierce" and also the one who "watches over all people". The old commentator explains that this watching is a looking at what each person has done, good and bad. The prayer ends by saying that the worshippers serve Death with offerings. It belongs to a group of short prayers and offering formulas near the end of the Upaniṣad that ask for protection and for release from wrongdoing. The edition reports what the words say and what the commentator says they are for; it makes no claim about what reciting them does.
analogy: Like a petition placed before a stern magistrate: it names, one by one, each thing it asks him not to take.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It addresses Death twice, as mṛtyu and as ugra, ‘fierce’, and forbids five actions: cutting off, striking, tearing away strength, carrying it off, and harming offspring and life. It closes by declaring that the speakers serve him with oblation, calling him nṛcakṣas, ‘the watcher of people’.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator calls Death «हे मृत्यो हे उग्र क्रूर» — O Death, O fierce, cruel one. He supplies what is to be spared: our performance of good works («अस्मत्सत्कर्मानुष्ठानं मा वधीर्मा हिंसय»), bodily strength («मे मम शारीरं बलं मा विवृहो मा पीडय») and our means to the next world («अस्मदीयपरलोकसाधनं मा प्रमोषीर्मा चोरव»). He explains nṛcakṣas as one who looks at living beings to examine their merit and sin: «नृन्प्राणिनश्चष्टे पुण्यपापरीक्षायै पश्यतीति नृचक्षास्तं नृचक्षसम्». The oblation is the reason Death is asked to spare them: «तदर्थ त्वा त्वां हविषा», ‘for that, [we serve] you with oblation’.

commentary.q: Why are all the verbs aorists without the augment?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Sanskrit forbids with mā and an aorist, P. 3.3.175 (माङि लुङ्), and after mā the aorist takes no augment, P. 6.4.74 (न माङ्योगे): so chidaḥ, not acchidaḥ; vadhīḥ, not avadhīḥ. Five such forms in two lines give the prayer its insistent rhythm.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among them). The anonymous bhāṣya explains the words and the rite; it does not argue an Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita position here, so the edition gives none.

contemporary.text: The prayer does not argue with death or deny it; it names what a person most fears to lose — strength, children, life — and asks that these be spared for now. Naming what is at stake is itself a way of facing it. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Of the five things the prayer asks Death not to take, which would you have put first?
reflect.deeper: The commentator reads ‘do not strike’ as ‘do not destroy our good works’ and ‘do not carry off’ as ‘do not take our means to the next world’. What does that reading add to the plain words?
reflect.practice: Write down three things you would not want to lose, and one thing you do each day that protects them.

references.text: No comment of Sāyaṇa’s or Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources: Sāyaṇa’s anuvākas 52–57 are missing from the digital text used here, and neither commentary file glosses these words; the edition’s concordance maps give no anuvāka of theirs for it. The anonymous bhāṣya is the only commentary quoted.

flags.note: The Tirupati e-text lacks विधेम at the end of this anuvāka and prints it at the start of the next: a matter of where that e-text draws the anuvāka boundary, not a different reading (corrections.json lists both sides).
The source of this verse outside the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka is not established from the edition’s sources, so no parallel is cited.
